title: How to compress a file in Finder on Mac: steps, shortcut limits and fixes
metaTitle: How to Compress a File in Finder on Mac (Step by Step)
description: Compress a file in Finder on Mac by Control-clicking it and choosing Compress. Learn the zip names, shortcut limits and the permission fix that stops it.

intro: To compress a file in Finder on Mac, Control-click the file and choose Compress from the shortcut menu. Finder makes a .zip file named after the item, or Archive.zip when you select several items at once.
tldr: Select the file or folder in Finder, then Control-click it and choose Compress.
One item becomes a .zip with the same name, such as Report.pdf.zip. Several items become Archive.zip.
Apple's keyboard shortcut list has no shortcut for Compress, and Finder's Compress has no password option.
If Compress fails, open Get Info, expand Sharing & Permissions, and set your access to Read & Write.

blocks.text: Why compress a file in Finder on Mac

Compressing packs a file or folder into one .zip archive. A single archive is easier to email, upload or move than a pile of loose files. It also keeps related items together. You don't need another app for this. Finder does it from the menu you already use.

Large files cause real friction. A survey of 1,001 full-time US employees, sponsored by Smallpdf, found that 78% had at least one work problem caused by large files. The same survey found that 51% would compress files more often if it were easier. Read those numbers as a sign of a common problem, not a precise measure, because the sponsor has a stake in the answer.
What the new zip file is called

Finder follows a simple rule. A single item keeps its name and gets .zip added. Report.pdf becomes Report.pdf.zip, and a folder called Invoices becomes Invoices.zip. Several items go into one file called Archive.zip. Apple's zip guide describes both cases.

blocks.caption: Names come from Apple's zip guide. Menu labels come from Donemax and may differ on your Mac.

blocks.text: Rename the archive as soon as it appears. Archive.zip tells you nothing about its contents. If you make several archives from one folder, generic names make them hard to sort. A name such as client-photos-march.zip saves time later.
Compress a folder or several items

Folders use the same command. Control-click the folder in a Finder window or on the desktop, then choose Compress. Apple's guide covers both places, so you don't need to move the folder first. Everything inside the folder goes into the archive, including any subfolders.
Before you compress a folder, open it and look inside. Remove anything you don't want to send, or move it out first. The zip contains whatever is in the folder when you compress it.

To compress several items, select them all first. Click the first item, then hold Command and click each one you want. Control-click any highlighted item and choose Compress. Finder builds one archive for the whole selection.

blocks.title: Check the size before you send
blocks.text: Photos and video files are already compressed, so a .zip may barely shrink them. Select the .zip and press Command-I to check its size in Get Info before you send it.
Compress files for email and sharing

Say you need to send a folder of project files by email. Compress the folder first, then attach the single .zip. The recipient gets one attachment instead of many. Name the archive after the project, so the recipient knows what it holds.

Some mail services limit attachment sizes. Check the limit for your service before you attach a large archive. A .zip won't shrink much if the files inside are already compressed, so the total size may stay about the same.

items: Compress when you send many files as one package, such as a project folder.
Skip compressing when the recipient needs to open one file quickly, such as a single PDF.
Compress when the files must stay grouped, because the archive keeps them together.
Check the size with Get Info before you send, and split the work if the archive is too large for your mail service.

blocks.text: Keyboard shortcuts for Finder and compressing
Apple's Mac keyboard shortcuts list has no shortcut for Compress. The list does include shortcuts for file tasks near compressing. Learn these first, because they save clicks while you prepare files.

blocks.caption: Shortcuts from Apple's Mac keyboard shortcuts page. Compress is not on that list.

blocks.text: Some people try to build their own shortcut for Compress. A 2015 Apple Community thread describes a custom shortcut for a compress action on Mac OS X 10.7.5. It showed up in the right-click menu, but the keys did nothing. Test any custom shortcut on your own Mac before you rely on it.
Password protecting a zip file

Finder's Compress command has no password option, and Apple's steps don't add one. If you need a password on the archive, Finder alone won't do it. Third-party guides, such as Donemax's, cover password-protected zips. Apple's own pages don't confirm those routes.

Search results disagreed about whether Archive Utility can set a password. The Apple pages checked for this guide didn't settle it. This guide won't give a password workaround it can't confirm. Check Apple's current Mac User Guide before you send sensitive files.
When Finder won't compress the item

The most common cause is permissions. Apple's troubleshooting page says that if you can't compress a file or folder, you may not have the access level you need. The fix happens in Get Info, not in the compression menu.
Apple's guide doesn't list a specific error message. Match the symptom instead. If Finder refuses to create the zip, check permissions before you try anything else.
Check and change permissions in Get Info

items: Click the item once to select it, then choose File > Get Info or press Command-I.
Click the arrow beside Sharing & Permissions to show the list.
Find your access level in the pop-up next to your user name.
If the settings are locked, click the lock and enter an administrator's name and password. Touch ID or Apple Watch can also authorize.
Set the permission to Read & Write, or Read only, then return to Finder and try Compress again.

blocks.text: Read & Write is the setting you need to create a new archive in that folder. Read only lets you look at the contents but blocks new files. If you can't change the permission, Apple says to ask a Mac administrator or the owner of the file or folder. On a work Mac, that is often your IT team.
Unzip the archive on the other end
Unzipping works from the other side. Double-click the .zip file. Apple's zip guide says the extracted item appears in the same folder as the archive.
If the archive won't open, Apple suggests two checks. Make sure you have enough free disk space. Or ask the sender to zip the files again. Try both before you decide the archive is broken.
Common mistakes to avoid

items: Compressing the wrong selection. Look inside folders first, then select only what you want to send.
Expecting a password option. Finder's Compress doesn't ask for one.
Ignoring read-only folders. A folder you can't write to will block the new archive.
Deleting originals before you test. Unzip the archive once, then remove files you no longer need.
Leaving the name as Archive.zip. A clear name saves the next person a search.

blocks.text: Compress on iCloud.com or an iPhone

This guide covers Finder on the Mac. Apple's compression help covers Finder and the Files app on iPhone. The pages checked for this guide don't confirm how iCloud.com handles zip files. Don't assume the Mac steps carry over to a browser.
What to do next

Once your archive is ready, you may want to find it again. A tag makes a batch of archives easy to filter. See [How to add a tag to a file in Finder on Mac](/how-to/add-a-tag-to-a-file-in-finder) for the steps.

Before you compress a file, you may want to check its contents. The [preview pane guide](/how-to/use-the-preview-pane-in-finder) shows how to look at a file in Finder without opening it in another app.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut to compress a file on Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's Mac keyboard shortcuts list has no shortcut for Compress. Use Control-click, then choose Compress. A custom shortcut is possible, but test it first, because a 2015 Apple Community report describes one that did nothing.

faq.question: What is the name of the zip file Finder creates?
faq.answer: A single item keeps its name and gets .zip added, so Report.pdf becomes Report.pdf.zip. Several items go into one file called Archive.zip. Rename it right after you create it.

faq.question: Can I compress a folder on the desktop?
faq.answer: Yes. Apple's zip guide says you can Control-click a file or folder in Finder or on the desktop and choose Compress. Everything inside the folder goes into the archive.

faq.question: Why does Finder say it can't compress a file?
faq.answer: Permissions are the usual cause. Select the item, press Command-I, expand Sharing & Permissions, and set your access to Read & Write. Ask an administrator if you can't change it.

faq.question: Can I add a password when I compress in Finder?
faq.answer: Finder's Compress command doesn't offer a password option, and Apple's steps don't add one. Check Apple's current guide before you use a password method from another source.

faq.question: Does this work on iCloud.com?
faq.answer: This guide covers Finder on the Mac. The pages checked for it don't confirm how iCloud.com handles zip files, so test a small file before you rely on the browser.

faq.question: Do I need to install anything to compress a file?
faq.answer: No. Control-click and Compress are part of Finder on macOS, so you don't install an app. Third-party zip apps exist, but the steps on this page use only Finder.

steps.name: Open Finder and find the item
steps.text: Click the Finder icon in the Dock to open a window. Browse to the file or folder. You can also use an item on your desktop.
steps.tip: Apple's zip guide says you can compress in Finder or on the desktop.

steps.name: Select the file or folder
steps.text: Click the item once so it is highlighted. For several items, hold Command and click each one you want.

steps.name: Control-click the selected item
steps.text: Hold Control and click the item. The shortcut menu opens. If your mouse or trackpad is set to right-click, use that instead.
steps.tip: If Compress doesn't show up, make sure the item is still selected.

steps.name: Choose Compress
steps.text: Click Compress in the shortcut menu. For a single item, Donemax describes the label as Compress followed by the file name. For several items, it reads Compress X Items. Your Mac may use either form.

steps.name: Check the new .zip file
steps.text: Finder creates the archive. One item keeps its name and gets .zip added. Several items go into Archive.zip. Look for the new file in the folder you are working in.

steps.name: Rename the archive
steps.text: Click the archive name once, type a clear name, and press Return. Keep the .zip ending so the file still opens as an archive.
steps.tip: A name such as project-files.zip is easier to find later than Archive.zip.

steps.name: Test the archive before you delete originals
steps.text: Double-click the .zip file. Apple says the extracted item appears in the same folder. Open the extracted files to confirm they work. Then delete the originals only if you no longer need them.
steps.tip: If the archive won't open, check free disk space first.

steps.name: Fix permissions if Compress fails
steps.text: Select the item and choose File > Get Info. Expand Sharing & Permissions, set your access to Read & Write, then try Compress again. Enter an administrator's name and password first if the settings are locked.

troubleshooting.problem: Can't compress a file or folder
troubleshooting.fix: Open Get Info and expand Sharing & Permissions. Read your access level in the pop-up next to your user name, then set it to Read & Write. Enter an administrator's name and password first if the setting is locked.
Ask a Mac administrator or the owner of the file or folder to change it, as Apple's troubleshooting page advises.
Click the item itself so it stays selected, then Control-click again. Apple's guide doesn't cover a missing menu item, so check the Mac User Guide if it still doesn't appear.
Check free disk space, then ask the sender to zip the files again if it still fails. Those are the two checks Apple suggests.

troubleshooting.problem: I need a password on the zip
troubleshooting.fix: Finder's Compress has no password option. Third-party guides cover password zips, but Apple's pages don't confirm those methods, so check Apple's current guide before you rely on one.
Test it on your own Mac first. A 2015 Apple Community report describes a custom compress shortcut that showed up in the menu but did nothing, so keep Control-click as the fallback.
